<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:diam2}
Every connected cograph on at least two vertices has diameter at most $2$. Consequently, every connected $\mathcal{C}$-graph satisfies
\[
D(G) = 2(J-I) - A(G),
\]
where $J$ is the all-ones matrix.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
A connected cograph on $\ge 2$ vertices is, by the defining recursive structure, a join $G = G_1 \vee G_2$ of two smaller cographs. Two vertices in different parts are adjacent; two vertices in the same part are joined by a path of length $2$ through any vertex of the other part. Hence $\operatorname{diam}(G) \le 2$. The formula for $D(G)$ follows immediately: $D_{ij} = 1$ if $ij \in E(G)$ and $D_{ij}=2$ otherwise, for $i \ne j$.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:master}
If $G$ is a connected graph with $\operatorname{diam}(G)\le 2$ on $n$ vertices, then
\[
D^L(G) = 2nI - 2J - L(G).
\]
Consequently,
\[
\operatorname{spec}(D^L(G)) = \{0\} \cup \{\, 2n - \mu : \mu \in \operatorname{spec}^*(L(G)) \,\}.
\]
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
By Lemma \ref{lem:diam2}, $D(G) = 2J - 2I - A(G)$, so $\operatorname{Tr}_i = \sum_{j\ne i} D_{ij} = 2(n-1) - \deg(i)$, giving $\operatorname{Tr}(G) = 2(n-1)I - \deg(G)$. Then
\[
D^L(G) = \operatorname{Tr}(G) - D(G) = \big[2(n-1)I - \deg(G)\big] - \big[2J-2I-A(G)\big] = 2nI - 2J - \big(\deg(G)-A(G)\big) = 2nI-2J-L(G).
\]
The spectral statement follows because $\mathbf{1}$ is a common eigenvector of $J$ (eigenvalue $n$) and $L(G)$ (eigenvalue $0$), while every eigenvector of $L(G)$ orthogonal to $\mathbf 1$ lies in the kernel of $J$.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
Lemma \ref{lem:master} holds for \emph{any} connected diameter-$2$ graph, not just cographs; see \cite{AouchicheHansen2013}. What is special to $\mathcal{C}$-graphs is that $L(G)$ itself is fully computable from the creation sequence, as we show next.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:laprecursion}
Let $S_i$ denote the Laplacian spectrum (as a multiset) of $G_i = C(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_i)$. Then $S_1 = \{0^{(\alpha_1)}\}$ and, for $i\ge 2$,
\[
S_i = \{0\} \;\cup\; \{\, n_i - \theta : \theta \in S_{i-1} \,\} \;\cup\; \{\, n_{i-1}^{\,(\alpha_i-1)} \,\}.
\]
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:closedform}
An eigenvalue born at step $b$ with value $v \in \{0, n_{b-1}\}$ propagates to the final eigenvalue
\[
\lambda(b,v) =
\begin{cases}
v + \displaystyle\sum_{\substack{j=b+2 \\ j \equiv b \ (2)}}^{m} \alpha_j, & m-b \text{ even},\\[3mm]
n_m - v - \displaystyle\sum_{\substack{j=b+2 \\ j\equiv b\ (2)}}^{m-1} \alpha_j, & m-b \text{ odd},
\end{cases}
\]
and $\operatorname{spec}(L(G))$ is exactly the multiset of all such $\lambda(b,v)$, taken with the stated multiplicities.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Track the value born at step $b$ through the transformation $\theta \mapsto n_j - \theta$ applied once at each subsequent step $j = b+1,\dots,m$ (Theorem \ref{thm:laprecursion}). This alternating reflection telescopes: two consecutive applications shift the value by $\alpha_{j}+\alpha_{j-1}$-type increments, giving the stated sum over indices of matching parity, with a final reflection through $n_m$ when an odd number of steps remain.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:integral}
For every $\mathcal{C}$-graph $G$, $\operatorname{spec}(L(G)) \subset \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$, and hence $\operatorname{spec}(D^L(G)) \subset \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Immediate from Theorem \ref{thm:closedform}: every value $\lambda(b,v)$ is an integer combination of the $\alpha_j \in \mathbb{N}$ and the partial sums $n_i$, hence an integer. (This also follows more generally, and without the explicit closed form, from Merris's theorem \cite{Merris1998} that every cograph is Laplacian-integral — $\mathcal{C}$-graphs being a special case.) Integrality of $\operatorname{spec}(D^L(G))$ follows from Lemma \ref{lem:master}, since $2n-\mu$ is an integer whenever $\mu$ and $n$ are.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- example-1: body_md -->
\label{ex:main}
For $G = C(4,3,2,2)$ ($n=11$), Theorem \ref{thm:closedform} gives
\[
\operatorname{spec}(L(G)) = \{0,\,2,\,4,\,6,\,6,\,9,\,9,\,9,\,9,\,9,\,11\},
\]
which was confirmed by direct diagonalization of $L(G)$. By Lemma \ref{lem:master},
\[
\operatorname{spec}(D^L(G)) = \{0\} \cup \{22-2,\,22-4,\,22-6,\,22-6,\,22-9^{(5)},\,22-11\} = \{0,\,11,\,13^{(5)},\,16^{(2)},\,18,\,20\},
\]
also confirmed directly.
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{thm:maxeig}
For every $\mathcal{C}$-graph $G = C(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_m)$ with $m\ge 2$, $\mu_{\max}(L(G)) = n$ exactly.
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
$G_m = H \vee \overline{K}_{\alpha_m}$ where $H = \overline{G_{m-1}}$, so $\overline{G_m} = G_{m-1} \cup K_{\alpha_m}$, a genuine disjoint union of two nonempty graphs, hence disconnected. Since $\mu_{\max}(L(G)) = n$ if and only if $\overline{G}$ is disconnected, the claim follows.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{thm:Lgap}
For every $\mathcal{C}$-graph $G=C(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_m)$ with $m\ge 2$, every eigenvalue of $L(G)$ other than $0$ and the maximum eigenvalue $n$ lies in $[\alpha_{\min}, n-\alpha_{\min}]$. Equivalently, $(0,\alpha_{\min}) \cup (n-\alpha_{\min}, n)$ is eigenvalue-free.
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
We induct on $m$. Write $G_m = H \vee \overline K_{\alpha_m}$, $H=\overline{G_{m-1}}$, $n(H)=n_{m-1}$. By the join formula,
\[
\operatorname{spec}^*(L(G_m)) \setminus \{n_m\} = \{n_{m-1}\}^{(\alpha_m-1)} \cup \{\alpha_m + \mu : \mu \in \operatorname{spec}^*(L(H))\}.
\]
\emph{Lower bound.} Since $\mu \ge 0$ always, $\alpha_m + \mu \ge \alpha_m \ge \alpha_{\min}$, and $n_{m-1} \ge \alpha_{\min}$ trivially (it is a sum of at least one $\alpha_j$). This gives the lower bound with no induction required.

\emph{Upper bound.} By the inductive hypothesis applied to $G_{m-1}$ (with $\beta := \min(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_{m-1}) \ge \alpha_{\min}$), every eigenvalue of $L(G_{m-1})$ other than $0$ and $n_{m-1}$ lies in $[\beta, n_{m-1}-\beta]$. Applying the complementation rule $\operatorname{spec}(L(H)) = \{0\} \cup \{n_{m-1}-\theta : \theta \in \operatorname{spec}^*(L(G_{m-1}))\}$, the interval $[\beta,n_{m-1}-\beta]$ is symmetric under $\theta \mapsto n_{m-1}-\theta$ and hence maps to itself; the single eigenvalue $\theta = n_{m-1}$ of $G_{m-1}$ maps to $0$ (consistent with $H$ being disconnected). Thus every nonzero eigenvalue of $H$ satisfies $\mu \le n_{m-1}-\beta \le n_{m-1}-\alpha_{\min}$, so $\alpha_m + \mu \le n_{m-1}+\alpha_m-\alpha_{\min} = n_m - \alpha_{\min}$, completing the induction. The base case $m=2$ is verified directly.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{thm:main}
For every connected $\mathcal{C}$-graph $G=C(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_m)$ ($m\ge2$) on $n$ vertices,
\[
\operatorname{spec}^*(D^L(G)) \subseteq \{n\} \cup [\,n+\alpha_{\min},\ 2n-\alpha_{\min}\,],
\]
so that
\[
(0,n) \ \cup\ (n,\,n+\alpha_{\min}) \ \cup\ (2n-\alpha_{\min},\,2n)
\]
is an eigenvalue-free region for $D^L(G)$, with $n$ itself always an isolated eigenvalue.
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Immediate from Theorems \ref{thm:maxeig} and \ref{thm:Lgap} via the reflection $\mu \mapsto 2n-\mu$ of Lemma \ref{lem:master}: $\mu=n \mapsto n$, and $\mu \in [\alpha_{\min}, n-\alpha_{\min}] \mapsto 2n-\mu \in [n+\alpha_{\min}, 2n-\alpha_{\min}]$.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- example-2: body_md -->
Continuing Example \ref{ex:main} ($n=11$, $\alpha_{\min}=2$): Theorem \ref{thm:main} predicts $\operatorname{spec}^*(D^L) \subseteq \{11\}\cup[n+\alpha_{\min},\,2n-\alpha_{\min}] = \{11\}\cup[13,20]$. The actual spectrum $\{11,\,13^{(5)},\,16^{(2)},\,18,\,20\}$ lies entirely within this predicted region, and the bound is tight: the top eigenvalue $20 = 2n-\alpha_{\min}$ is attained exactly.
<!-- end example-2 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
\label{thm:multformula}
Let $G=C(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_m)$ be a connected $\mathcal{C}$-graph on $n$ vertices, and let $\theta \in \mathbb{R}$. Then $\mathrm{mult}_{D^L(G)}(0)=1$, and for $\theta \ne 0$, writing $\mu = 2n-\theta$,
\[
\mathrm{mult}_{D^L(G)}(\theta) \;=\; \sum_{\substack{(b,v)\; :\; \lambda(b,v) = \mu}} \mathrm{mult}(b,v),
\]
the sum ranging over all births $(b,v,\mathrm{mult}(b,v))$ of Theorem \ref{thm:closedform} whose propagated value $\lambda(b,v)$ equals $\mu$. This determines $\mathrm{mult}_{D^L(G)}(\theta)$ in $O(m)$ arithmetic operations, with no matrix computation required.
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Immediate from Lemma \ref{lem:master} ($\theta\ne0$ is a $D^L(G)$-eigenvalue of multiplicity equal to that of $\mu=2n-\theta$ as an $L(G)$-eigenvalue) together with Theorem \ref{thm:closedform}, which expresses $\operatorname{spec}(L(G))$ exactly as the multiset of propagated birth values.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- theorem-8: body_md -->
\label{thm:multofn}
For a connected $\mathcal{C}$-graph $G=C(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_m)$, $m\ge2$ even,
\[
\mathrm{mult}_{D^L(G)}(n) = \begin{cases} \alpha_1 & m=2,\\ 1 & m\ge 4.\end{cases}
\]
<!-- end theorem-8 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
By Lemma \ref{lem:master}, $\theta=n$ reflects to $\mu=2n-n=n=n_m$, so we must count births with $\lambda(b,v)=n_m$. If $m-b$ is even, $\lambda(b,v)=v+\Sigma \le n_{b-1} + \sum_{j=b+2}^{m}\alpha_j \le n_m - \alpha_b - \alpha_{b+1} < n_m$ (using $b\le m-2$, so both $\alpha_b,\alpha_{b+1}$ exist and are $\ge1$; the case $b=m$ gives $\lambda=v\in\{0,n_{m-1}\}$, neither equal to $n_m$), so no even-step birth reaches $n_m$. If $m-b$ is odd, $\lambda(b,v)=n_m-v-\Sigma=n_m$ forces $v=0$ and $\Sigma=0$; the latter requires the summation range $j=b+2,\dots,m-1$ (matching parity) to be empty, i.e.\ $b\ge m-2$, which combined with $m-b$ odd forces $b=m-1$ uniquely. For $m\ge4$, $b=m-1\ge3\ge2$ lies in the generic regime of Theorem \ref{thm:closedform}, where the $v=0$ birth at step $b$ always carries multiplicity $1$. For $m=2$, $b=m-1=1$ coincides with the base case $b=1$, whose birth $(v=0)$ carries multiplicity $\alpha_1$ instead — recovering the classical complete split graph spectrum $(\alpha_1+\alpha_2)^{\alpha_1},\,\alpha_1^{\,\alpha_2-1},\,0$ for $L(C(\alpha_1,\alpha_2))$.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- example-3: body_md -->
For $G=C(4,3,2,2)$, Theorem \ref{thm:multformula} recovers every multiplicity in Example \ref{ex:main} directly: e.g.\ $\theta=13$ reflects to $\mu=22-13=9$, and Theorem \ref{thm:closedform} assigns multiplicity $5$ to $\mu=9$, matching $\operatorname{spec}(D^L(G))$ above. Since $m=4\ge4$, Theorem \ref{thm:multofn} predicts $\mathrm{mult}_{D^L(G)}(n)=\mathrm{mult}_{D^L(G)}(11)=1$, also matching. By contrast, for $C(3,5)$ ($m=2$, $n=8$), Theorem \ref{thm:multofn} predicts $\mathrm{mult}_{D^L(G)}(8)=\alpha_1=3$, confirmed by direct computation.
<!-- end example-3 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
Theorem \ref{thm:multofn} shows that the maximum eigenvalue $\theta=n$, while always \emph{isolated} (separated from the rest of the spectrum by the gap $(n,n+\alpha_{\min})$), is \emph{simple} only for $m\ge4$; for $m=2$ its multiplicity equals $\alpha_1$ and can be arbitrarily large. This refines the parenthetical remark in Theorem \ref{thm:main}.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- theorem-9: body_md -->
\label{thm:distincteig}
For every connected $\mathcal{C}$-graph $G=C(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_m)$, $s(D^L(G)) = s(L(G))$. Consequently,
\[
m \;\le\; s(D^L(G)) \;\le\; 2m-1,
\]
and both bounds are sharp.
<!-- end theorem-9 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
By Lemma \ref{lem:master}, $\operatorname{spec}(D^L(G)) = \{0\} \cup \{2n-\mu : \mu \in \operatorname{spec}^*(L(G))\}$. The map $\mu \mapsto 2n-\mu$ is a strictly monotonic bijection of $\mathbb{R}$, so it carries distinct values of $\operatorname{spec}^*(L(G))$ to distinct values of $\operatorname{spec}^*(D^L(G))$, giving $|\operatorname{spec}^*(D^L(G))| = |\operatorname{spec}^*(L(G))|$ as sets. Since every eigenvalue of $L(G)$ satisfies $\mu \le n$ (Theorem \ref{thm:maxeig}), every reflected value satisfies $2n-\mu \ge n > 0$, so $0$ can never coincide with a reflected value; hence $s(D^L(G)) = 1 + |\operatorname{spec}^*(D^L(G))| = 1 + |\operatorname{spec}^*(L(G))| = s(L(G))$. The bounds and their sharpness now follow directly from \cite[Thm.\ 4.1]{MMS2024}.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- example-4: body_md -->
The lower bound is attained by $C(\alpha_1,1,\dots,1)$: e.g.\ $C(5,1,1,1)$ ($m=4$) has $s(D^L(G))=4=m$. The upper bound is attained by any complete split graph $C(\alpha_1,\alpha_2)$ ($m=2$, giving $s(D^L(G))=3=2m-1$ always) and, for larger $m$, by $C(5,2,3,4,2,8)$ ($m=6$), which achieves $s(D^L(G))=11=2m-1$ — the same sequence Mandal, Mehatari and Stani\'c use to witness sharpness for $s(L(G))$ in \cite[Remark 4.3]{MMS2024}. For the constant sequence $C(p,\dots,p)$ ($m$ times, $p\ne1$), \cite[Thm.\ 4.4]{MMS2024} gives $s(L(G))=m+1$, and Theorem \ref{thm:distincteig} transfers this unchanged to $s(D^L(G))=m+1$; confirmed directly for $(p,m)\in\{(4,4),(3,6),(5,4),(2,8)\}$.
<!-- end example-4 -->
<!-- theorem-10: body_md -->
\label{thm:polymaster}
Write $\chi_{L(G)}(y) = y\,\psi(y)$, where $\psi$ is the degree-$(n-1)$ polynomial collecting the nonzero eigenvalues of $L(G)$. Then the characteristic polynomial of $D^L(G)$ is
\[
\chi_{D^L(G)}(x) \;=\; (-1)^{n-1}\, x\, \psi(2n-x) \;=\; (-1)^{n-1}\,\frac{x}{2n-x}\,\chi_{L(G)}(2n-x),
\]
the division being exact as polynomials.
<!-- end theorem-10 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
By Lemma \ref{lem:master}, $\operatorname{spec}(D^L(G)) = \{0\}\cup\{2n-\mu : \mu \in \operatorname{spec}^*(L(G))\}$. For each nonzero eigenvalue $\mu$ of $L(G)$,
\[
x - (2n-\mu) = \mu - (2n-x) = -\big((2n-x)-\mu\big),
\]
so $\prod_{\mu \in \operatorname{spec}^*(L(G))} \big(x-(2n-\mu)\big) = (-1)^{n-1}\prod_{\mu\in\operatorname{spec}^*(L(G))}\big((2n-x)-\mu\big) = (-1)^{n-1}\psi(2n-x)$. Multiplying by the factor $x$ contributed by the isolated $0$-eigenvalue of $D^L(G)$ gives $\chi_{D^L(G)}(x) = (-1)^{n-1}x\,\psi(2n-x)$. Since $\chi_{L(G)}(2n-x) = (2n-x)\,\psi(2n-x)$, the second equality follows, and the division by $2n-x$ is exact because $\psi$ is itself a polynomial.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- theorem-11: body_md -->
\label{thm:polyexplicit}
With $\lambda(b,v)$ as in Theorem \ref{thm:closedform},
\[
\chi_{D^L(G)}(x) = x\cdot\prod_{b=2}^{m}\Big(x-\big(2n-\lambda(b,0)\big)\Big)\cdot\prod_{b=2}^{m}\Big(x-\big(2n-\lambda(b,n_{b-1})\big)\Big)^{\alpha_b-1}.
\]
<!-- end theorem-11 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
Immediate from Theorem \ref{thm:closedform} together with the reflection $\mu\mapsto 2n-\mu$ of Lemma \ref{lem:master}, applied term-by-term to the multiset of births.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- example-5: body_md -->
For $G=C(4,3,2,2)$ ($n=11$), Theorem \ref{thm:polyexplicit} (equivalently, reflecting the spectrum of Example \ref{ex:main}) gives the factored form
\[
\chi_{D^L(G)}(x) = x(x-11)(x-13)^5(x-16)^2(x-18)(x-20),
\]
which expands to
\[
x^{11}-146x^{10}+9557x^9-369390x^8+9336643x^7-161266918x^6+1927856463x^5
\]
\[
-15751245146x^4+84182273240x^3-265769929984x^2+376401991680\,x.
\]
This was independently confirmed three ways: by direct diagonalization of $D^L(G)$, by applying Theorem \ref{thm:polymaster} to the directly computed $\chi_{L(G)}$, and by the explicit product of Theorem \ref{thm:polyexplicit} — all three agree exactly.
<!-- end example-5 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
Theorem \ref{thm:polyexplicit} requires no computation of $L(G)$, $A(G)$, or any matrix at all: every coefficient of $\chi_{D^L(G)}$ is obtained in $O(m)$ arithmetic operations directly from the creation sequence $(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_m)$, in the same spirit as the tridiagonal-determinant formula Mandal and Mehatari obtain for $\chi_{A(G)}$ in \cite[Thm.\ 4.1]{MM2025}, though here the closed form for the spectrum makes the polynomial available directly as a product rather than via a determinant recursion.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- theorem-12: body_md -->
\label{thm:DQlocal}
Let $G=C(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_m)$ be a connected $\mathcal{C}$-graph. For each block $C_i$ with $\alpha_i\ge2$,
\[
\operatorname{Tr}_i - 1 \text{ is an eigenvalue of } D^Q(G) \text{ with multiplicity} \ge \alpha_i-1 \text{ if } i \text{ is odd (clique block)},
\]
\[
\operatorname{Tr}_i - 2 \text{ is an eigenvalue of } D^Q(G) \text{ with multiplicity} \ge \alpha_i-1 \text{ if } i \text{ is even (independent block)}.
\]
<!-- end theorem-12 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
Let $u,v \in C_i$. Since $\operatorname{Tr}(G)$ is constant on $C_i$ and, in a diameter-$2$ graph, twins have identical distances to every vertex outside $C_i$, the vector $x=e_u-e_v$ satisfies $\operatorname{Tr}(G)x = \operatorname{Tr}_i\, x$ and $(D(G)x)_w = 0$ for $w\notin\{u,v\}$. If $C_i$ is a clique, $D(u,v)=1$, so $(D(G)x)_u = -1,\ (D(G)x)_v=1$, giving $D(G)x=-x$; if $C_i$ is independent, $D(u,v)=2$ (diameter $2$), giving $D(G)x=-2x$. Hence $D^Q(G)x = (\operatorname{Tr}_i\mp1\text{ or }2)x$ as claimed, and the $\alpha_i-1$ independent difference vectors within $C_i$ give the stated multiplicity.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:blockadjacency}
Let $G=C(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_m)$, $m$ even. For blocks $i<j$, every vertex of $C_i$ is adjacent to every vertex of $C_j$ if $j$ is even, and no vertex of $C_i$ is adjacent to any vertex of $C_j$ if $j$ is odd.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- theorem-13: body_md -->
\label{thm:DQquotient}
The equitable partition $\{C_1,\dots,C_m\}$ gives $D^Q(G)$ an $m\times m$ quotient matrix $Q_{D^Q}$ (in the sense of Godsil--Royle, so every eigenvalue of $Q_{D^Q}$ is an eigenvalue of $D^Q(G)$), with entries
\[
Q_{D^Q}(i,i) = \operatorname{Tr}_i + (\alpha_i-1)\cdot\begin{cases}1 & i \text{ odd}\\ 2 & i\text{ even}\end{cases},
\qquad
Q_{D^Q}(i,j) = \alpha_j\cdot\begin{cases}1 & \max(i,j)\text{ even}\\ 2 & \max(i,j)\text{ odd}\end{cases}\ (i\ne j).
\]
Together with Theorem \ref{thm:DQlocal} (with equality in the multiplicities), this accounts for the full spectrum of $D^Q(G)$: the $m$ eigenvalues of $Q_{D^Q}$ together with the $n-m$ local eigenvalues.
<!-- end theorem-13 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
The diagonal entry is the row sum of $D^Q(G)$ from a representative $u\in C_i$ into $C_i$ itself: $\operatorname{Tr}_i$ (the $u$-$u$ term) plus $(\alpha_i-1)$ terms of $D(u,v)=1$ or $2$ according to whether $C_i$ is a clique or independent set. The off-diagonal entry is the row sum from $u\in C_i$ into $C_j$: $\alpha_j$ vertices, each at distance $1$ or $2$ according to Proposition \ref{prop:blockadjacency}. That every eigenvalue of $Q_{D^Q}$ lifts to $D^Q(G)$ is the standard equitable-partition fact used throughout \cite{MM2025,MMS2024}.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- example-6: body_md -->
\label{ex:DQ}
For $G=C(4,3,2,2)$ ($n=11$): $d=(8,6,3,9)$, $\operatorname{Tr}=(12,14,17,11)$, and
\[
Q_{D^Q} = \begin{pmatrix}15&3&4&2\\4&18&4&2\\8&6&18&2\\4&3&2&13\end{pmatrix},
\]
which is \emph{not symmetric} (block sizes differ), with eigenvalues $\{10.049,\,12.432,\,13.812,\,27.707\}$. Combined with the local eigenvalues $\{9,\,11^{(3)},\,12^{(2)},\,16\}$ from Theorem \ref{thm:DQlocal}, this reproduces $\operatorname{spec}(D^Q(G))$ exactly, confirmed against direct diagonalization.
<!-- end example-6 -->
<!-- theorem-14: body_md -->
\label{thm:DQdistinctbound}
	For every connected $\mathcal{C}$-graph $G=C(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_m)$, $s(D^Q(G)) \le 2m$.
<!-- end theorem-14 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
By Theorem \ref{thm:DQquotient}, $\operatorname{spec}(D^Q(G))$ is exactly the union of the eigenvalues of $Q_{D^Q}$ (an $m\times m$ matrix, hence at most $m$ distinct values) and the local eigenvalues of Theorem \ref{thm:DQlocal} (one value, $\operatorname{Tr}_i-1$ or $\operatorname{Tr}_i-2$, per block with $\alpha_i\ge2$ — at most $m$ blocks, hence at most $m$ distinct values, irrespective of each value's multiplicity $\alpha_i-1$). A union of two sets of size $\le m$ has size $\le 2m$.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- theorem-15: body_md -->
\label{thm:DQpoly}
For a connected $\mathcal{C}$-graph $G=C(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_m)$,
\[
\chi_{D^Q(G)}(x) = \det(xI_m - Q_{D^Q})\cdot\!\!\prod_{\substack{i\text{ odd}\\\alpha_i\ge2}}\!\!\big(x-(\operatorname{Tr}_i-1)\big)^{\alpha_i-1}\cdot\!\!\prod_{\substack{i\text{ even}\\\alpha_i\ge2}}\!\!\big(x-(\operatorname{Tr}_i-2)\big)^{\alpha_i-1}.
\]
<!-- end theorem-15 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
Immediate from Theorem \ref{thm:DQquotient}: the characteristic polynomial factors as the product over the $m$ quotient eigenvalues and the $n-m$ local eigenvalues.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- theorem-16: body_md -->
\label{thm:DQgershgorin}
	For every connected $\mathcal{C}$-graph $G$, $\operatorname{spec}(D^Q(G)) \subseteq [0,\ 2\operatorname{Tr}_{\max}]$.
<!-- end theorem-16 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
Since $D^Q(G)(u,u)=\operatorname{Tr}_u$ and $\sum_{v\ne u} D^Q(G)(u,v) = \sum_{v\ne u} D(u,v) = \operatorname{Tr}_u$ (as $D(u,u)=0$), the Gershgorin disc at row $u$ is $[\operatorname{Tr}_u-\operatorname{Tr}_u,\ \operatorname{Tr}_u+\operatorname{Tr}_u]=[0,2\operatorname{Tr}_u]$. The union of these discs over all $u$ is $[0,2\operatorname{Tr}_{\max}]$, and every eigenvalue lies in this union.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- theorem-17: body_md -->
\label{thm:DQperron}
	$\mu_{\max}(D^Q(G)) \ge 2\operatorname{Tr}_{\min}$.
<!-- end theorem-17 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
The quotient matrix $Q_{D^Q}$ of Theorem \ref{thm:DQquotient} is entrywise nonnegative, and its $i$-th row sum equals the full row sum of $D^Q(G)$ at any representative of block $i$ (by construction of the quotient matrix), which is $2\operatorname{Tr}_i$. By the standard bound for nonnegative matrices, the spectral radius of $Q_{D^Q}$ — which is an eigenvalue of $D^Q(G)$, hence $\le\mu_{\max}(D^Q(G))$ — is at least the smallest row sum, $2\operatorname{Tr}_{\min}$.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:Trbound}
	For every connected graph $G$ with $\operatorname{diam}(G)\le2$, $\operatorname{Tr}_{\max}(G) \le 2\,\operatorname{Tr}_{\min}(G)$.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
Since $\operatorname{Tr}_i = 2(n-1)-d_i$, we have $\operatorname{Tr}_{\max}=2(n-1)-d_{\min}$ and $\operatorname{Tr}_{\min}=2(n-1)-d_{\max}$, so
	\[
	2\operatorname{Tr}_{\min} - \operatorname{Tr}_{\max} = 2(n-1) - 2d_{\max} + d_{\min} \ge 2(n-1) - 2(n-1) + d_{\min} = d_{\min} \ge 0,
	\]
	using $d_{\max}\le n-1$.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:localbound}
	Every local eigenvalue of $D^Q(G)$ (Theorem \ref{thm:DQlocal}) is strictly less than $2\operatorname{Tr}_{\min}$.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
Each local eigenvalue is $\operatorname{Tr}_i-1$ or $\operatorname{Tr}_i-2$ for some block $i$, hence $\le\operatorname{Tr}_{\max}-1 < \operatorname{Tr}_{\max} \le 2\operatorname{Tr}_{\min}$ by Lemma \ref{lem:Trbound}.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- theorem-18: body_md -->
\label{thm:DQgapthm}
	For every connected $\mathcal{C}$-graph $G$, every eigenvalue of $D^Q(G)$ other than $\mu_{\max}(D^Q(G))$ satisfies $\theta \le 2\operatorname{Tr}_{\min}$. Consequently
	\[
	\big(2\operatorname{Tr}_{\min},\ \mu_{\max}(D^Q(G))\big)
	\]
	is eigenvalue-free whenever non-empty.
<!-- end theorem-18 -->
<!-- example-7: body_md -->
For $G=C(4,3,2,2)$ (Example \ref{ex:DQ}), block transmissions are $\{11,12,14,17\}$, so $2\operatorname{Tr}_{\min}=22$ and $2\operatorname{Tr}_{\max}=34$. The actual spectrum $\{9,\,10.049,\,11^{(3)},\,12^{(2)},\,12.432,\,13.812,\,16,\,27.707\}$ satisfies $\operatorname{spec}\subset[0,34]$ (Theorem \ref{thm:DQgershgorin}), $\mu_{\max}=27.707 \ge 22$ (Theorem \ref{thm:DQperron}), and every other eigenvalue is $\le16 < 22$ — so $(22,\,27.707)$ is confirmed eigenvalue-free.
<!-- end example-7 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
For a graph $G$, define $u \preceq v$ if $N(u) \subseteq N[v]$ (equivalently, $N[u]\subseteq N[v]$ when $u\sim v$, and $N(u)\subseteq N(v)$ when $u\not\sim v$). This relation is reflexive and transitive (a \emph{preorder}), called the \emph{vicinal preorder}. A set of vertices pairwise related by $\preceq$ is a \emph{chain}; a set of pairwise unrelated is an \emph{antichain}. The \emph{Dilworth number} $\nabla(G)$ is the minimum number of chains needed to cover $V(G)$, equivalently (by Dilworth's theorem) the maximum size of an antichain.
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- theorem-19: body_md -->
\label{thm:LouLin}
	For a connected cograph $G$, the multiplicity of any eigenvalue of $D(G)$ other than $-2$ and $-1$ is at most $\nabla(G)$. Moreover, no connected cograph has a distance eigenvalue in the open interval $(-2,-1)$.
<!-- end theorem-19 -->
<!-- theorem-20: body_md -->
\label{thm:DLsimple}
	For every connected $\mathcal{C}$-graph $G$, every eigenvalue of $D^L(G)$ not in $\mathcal{T}^L(G)$ has multiplicity exactly $1$. In particular, $\mathrm{mult}_{D^L(G)}(\theta) \le \nabla(G)$ for all such $\theta$, but this bound is never tight unless $\nabla(G)=1$.
<!-- end theorem-20 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
By Lemma \ref{lem:master}, multiplicities transfer unchanged under $\mu\mapsto2n-\mu$ from $\operatorname{spec}(L(G))$ to $\operatorname{spec}(D^L(G))$. Every eigenvalue of $L(G)$ is either a local (twin-block) eigenvalue — exactly the values reflecting to $\mathcal{T}^L(G)$ — or an eigenvalue of the $m\times m$ quotient matrix $Q_L$, which by \cite[Cor.\ 3.4]{MMS2024} has $m$ \emph{pairwise distinct} eigenvalues. Hence any $\theta\notin\mathcal{T}^L(G)$ arises solely from a quotient eigenvalue and is therefore simple. Since $\nabla(G)\ge1$ always, $\mathrm{mult}(\theta)=1\le\nabla(G)$, with equality forced only when $\nabla(G)=1$.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- example-8: body_md -->
\label{ex:DQquotientrepeat}
	For $G=C(1,3,1,2)$ ($n=7$), the quotient matrix of Theorem \ref{thm:DQquotient} is
	\[
	Q_{D^Q} = \begin{pmatrix}7&3&2&2\\1&13&2&2\\2&6&10&2\\1&3&1&9\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \operatorname{spec}(Q_{D^Q}) = \{5.821,\ 8,\ 8,\ 17.179\},
	\]
	so $\theta=8$ is a genuinely repeated ($\mathrm{mult}=2$) eigenvalue of $D^Q(G)$, and $8\notin\mathcal{T}^Q(G)$ (it is not a local value for any block). Direct computation gives $\nabla(G)=2$ for this graph, so this instance attains the bound of Conjecture \ref{conj:DQdilworth} below with equality.
<!-- end example-8 -->
<!-- conjecture-1: body_md -->
\label{conj:DQdilworth}
	For every connected $\mathcal{C}$-graph $G$, every eigenvalue of $D^Q(G)$ not in $\mathcal{T}^Q(G)$ satisfies $\mathrm{mult}_{D^Q(G)}(\theta) \le \nabla(G)$.
<!-- end conjecture-1 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
This gives a precise answer to ``what is the relation between the Dilworth number and eigenvalue multiplicity'' for the two matrices: for $D^L(G)$, the Dilworth number is a valid but slack bound, since the true multiplicity of every non-trivial eigenvalue is exactly $1$ — a strictly stronger statement, provable outright from \cite[Cor.\ 3.4]{MMS2024}. For $D^Q(G)$, the Dilworth number is the correct and sharp governing quantity, because $D^Q(G)$'s quotient matrix lacks the simple-spectrum property that makes $D^L(G)$'s bound loose. This asymmetry traces directly to the structural asymmetry already noted in Section \ref{sec:DQ}: $L(G)$ commutes with $J$ (giving the master identity and, via \cite{MMS2024}, simple quotient eigenvalues), while $Q(G)$ does not.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
